# The Arrangement: Notes on Lichen

Lichen is easy to overlook. It crusts over gravestones and softens the north side of a stone wall. It hangs in pale beards from spruce branches and dusts park benches with a yellow-orange that might be paint or rust. Most people register it the way they register weather stains on a building: surface, patina, the look of something old. Almost no one stops to ask what it is.

The answer is strange, and it took scientists a long time and some bitter arguments to accept it.

## I. The Scandal of Two

For most of recorded history, naturalists assumed a lichen was a single organism, a plant of some humble kind, perhaps a relative of the mosses. Linnaeus grouped lichens with algae in a category he treated as the botanical lower orders, and he was not fond of them. He supposedly called them the "rustici pauperrimi," the poorest peasants of the vegetable kingdom. They seemed to do very little. They grew on nothing, ate nothing visible, and changed so slowly that one could watch a patch for years and see no difference.

In 1867 the Swiss botanist Simon Schwendener proposed that a lichen was not one thing at all. Looking closely at lichen tissue, he argued that it was a fungus and an alga living together. The fungus formed the body, the architecture, the part you see. Tucked inside, in a thin green layer just beneath the surface, were algal cells doing photosynthesis. The fungus, which cannot make its own food, was living on sugars produced by its photosynthetic partner.

Schwendener's framing did not help his reception. He described the relationship as a kind of enslavement: the fungus as master, the alga as captive, farmed and harvested. Lichenologists, many of whom had devoted their careers to classifying lichens as distinct species, were outraged. If a lichen was really two organisms, what exactly had they been naming? The idea was ridiculed as a "sensational romance" and an unnatural union. One critic compared it, with evident disgust, to a story about a captive maiden and a tyrant.

What makes the episode more than a footnote is what came out of the fight. In 1877 the German botanist Albert Bernhard Frank, thinking about lichens, needed a word for organisms of different kinds living intimately together without assuming one was simply exploiting the other. He coined *Symbiotismus*, which became "symbiosis." The concept now underlies much of biology: the mitochondria in our cells, the bacteria in our guts, the fungal networks tangled around tree roots, the origin of complex life itself. It came into the language because people were arguing about the crust on a rock.

Beatrix Potter got involved too, years before Peter Rabbit. She was a serious amateur mycologist who spent long hours drawing fungi and experimenting with spore germination, and she was persuaded by the dual hypothesis at a time when many established figures still resisted it. Her 1897 paper on spore germination was presented to the Linnean Society of London, though not by her. Women were not permitted to attend, so a man read it on her behalf. She eventually turned to children's books, where the botanical precision of her watercolors, all the moss and mushrooms and damp undergrowth, is easy to see once you know where it came from.

## II. The Scandal of Three

The story does not end with two.

In 2016 a team led by Toby Spribille published a paper showing that many lichens, including some of the most familiar and thoroughly studied species, contain a third partner: a yeast, a single-celled fungus of an entirely different lineage from the main fungal body, living in the lichen's outer layer. It had been there all along, in specimens that had been examined under microscopes for a century and a half. It was missed partly because nobody was looking for it, and partly because a lichen made of two things had become the textbook answer, and textbook answers are hard to see past.

This discovery made the question of what a lichen *is* more interesting, not less. Researchers increasingly describe lichens as ecosystems rather than organisms: a dominant fungus, one or more photosynthetic partners (sometimes green algae, sometimes cyanobacteria, sometimes both), various yeasts, and a whole community of bacteria. The lichen is less a creature than an arrangement, a stable pattern that forms when certain parties come together under certain conditions.

What grips me is that this arrangement has a consistent, recognizable shape. A given lichen species looks like itself. It has its characteristic color, its branching or leafy or crusty form, its particular chemistry. Yet no single partner "contains" that form. The main fungus, grown alone in a lab, does not build a lichen. It forms a shapeless lump. The alga grown alone just becomes algae. The lichen's shape exists only in the relationship. It is a property of the partnership, not of any partner.

We usually assume that identity lives inside things, that a creature's shape is written in its own instructions and simply unfolds. Lichens suggest another possibility: some forms exist only between things. Take away the relationship and the shape does not shrink or weaken. It stops existing.

## III. Slowness

Lichens are among the slowest-growing organisms on the planet. Some crustose lichens, the flat kind that look painted onto rock, grow a fraction of a millimeter a year. The map lichen, *Rhizocarpon geographicum*, gets its name from the way neighboring colonies meet in black boundary lines, so that a boulder covered in it looks like an atlas of yellow-green countries. It grows so slowly and steadily that geologists have used it as a clock. The technique, called lichenometry, measures the largest lichen colonies on rocks exposed by a retreating glacier or a rockfall and estimates how long the surface has been open to the air. The method has real uncertainties, since growth rates vary with climate and the curves need careful calibration, but it has helped date moraines and landslides where other methods fail.

Some lichen colonies are thought to be very old indeed. Estimates for certain Arctic and alpine specimens run into the thousands of years. The numbers are debated and I would not stake much on any specific figure, but the order of magnitude is not in dispute. There are lichens alive now that were already established when the pyramids were new or not yet begun. They have been sitting on their rocks, adding a sliver a year, through the entire span of written history.

I find it hard to hold that timescale in mind. Human attention is tuned to change. We notice what moves, what grows visibly, what responds. A lichen responds too, but on a register below our perception. It dries out completely in drought and becomes brittle and seemingly dead, then revives within minutes when rain comes and resumes photosynthesis. It can stay in that suspended state for long periods. It lives in pulses: wet and active, dry and dormant, wet again. Across centuries those pulses add up to a colony that is a record of every rain it has ever caught.

The slowness is not weakness. It is a strategy for places where nothing else can live. Lichens colonize bare rock, the raw surfaces left by glaciers and lava flows. They release acids that slowly etch the stone, and their dead tissue mixes with rock grains to make the first thin films of soil. Mosses follow, then small plants, then larger ones. Across much of the world's hard terrain, the long chain of life starts with a lichen patiently dissolving a mountain.

## IV. Endurance

It is almost a cliché now to say that lichens can survive anything, but the experimental record is impressive. In the 2000s the European Space Agency sent samples of lichens, including *Rhizocarpon geographicum* and *Xanthoria elegans*, a bright orange species common on rocks, into low Earth orbit and exposed them directly to space: vacuum, extreme temperature swings, and unfiltered cosmic and ultraviolet radiation. After days of exposure in one experiment, and much longer in later ones, many samples recovered their ability to photosynthesize once they were brought back and rehydrated. Lichens became one of the standard case studies for questions about whether life could survive in space or on the surface of Mars.

The mechanism is partly the same trick that gets them through desert droughts. A fully dried lichen is barely metabolizing at all, and in that state it can tolerate conditions that would destroy an active cell. The fungal cortex also contains pigments and compounds that act as sunscreen, shielding the photosynthetic partner beneath.

But the same organisms that can endure the vacuum of space are exquisitely sensitive to something far more ordinary: dirty air. Many lichens absorb water and nutrients directly from rain and atmosphere across their whole surface. They have no roots and no waxy cuticle to filter what comes in. Whatever is in the air ends up in the lichen. Sulfur dioxide in particular devastates them.

In the nineteenth century the Finnish botanist William Nylander noticed that lichens were disappearing from the Luxembourg Gardens in Paris as the city's air grew thick with coal smoke, and he suggested that lichens could serve as a kind of living gauge of air quality. That idea held up. Across industrial Europe, lichens vanished from city centers, leaving "lichen deserts" around factories and in urban cores. Researchers learned to map pollution by mapping which species survived where. When clean air laws came in and sulfur emissions fell, lichens began creeping back into cities. Some of the species people see on urban trees today are recolonists, returning to places they had been driven from generations before.

So a lichen can survive the harshest environment we know of and yet cannot survive a factory chimney. Toughness against extremes is one quality. Tolerance of chronic poisoning is another, and the lichen has only the first.

## V. What Lichens Carry

Because lichens take in whatever falls on them, they carry the history of their air. After the Chernobyl disaster in 1986, radioactive fallout drifted across Scandinavia. The reindeer lichens, the pale branching *Cladonia* species that carpet the northern tundra and forests, absorbed radioactive cesium from the rain. Reindeer depend on these lichens heavily in winter. The cesium moved from lichen to reindeer, and reindeer meat in parts of Norway and Sweden became contaminated, sometimes far above safety limits. For Sámi herders, whose economy and culture are bound up with reindeer, the consequences lasted for years. Because lichens grow so slowly, the contamination did not clear quickly. An accident in Ukraine rewrote the diet and livelihood of people more than a thousand kilometers away, through the slowest link in the food chain.

Lichens have carried more benign things into human life as well. For centuries they were a source of dyes. Orchil, a purple dye made from certain lichens, was valuable enough to be traded across the Mediterranean and beyond. Some Scottish tweeds were traditionally colored with lichen dyes, and the distinctive smell of certain old woolens has been attributed to it. Litmus, the pigment that turns red in acid and blue in base, the first chemistry experiment many children ever do, comes from lichens. Every school laboratory that has dipped a paper strip into vinegar has used a substance made by this partnership.

People have also eaten lichens, usually in hard times. Iceland moss, which is a lichen despite the name, was boiled into porridges and breads. There is a longstanding hypothesis, still speculative, that the biblical manna might have been a lichen that can detach and blow across desert terrain in clumps. I have no idea whether that is true, and I am wary of tidy explanations for ancient stories. But I like the image of a wind-borne lichen falling like food from the sky on people who had nothing else.

## VI. The Question of the Individual

I keep coming back to the question the nineteenth-century lichenologists fought over: what is the thing being named?

Biology has a strong habit of thinking in individuals. An organism has a boundary. Inside is self, outside is environment. It has one genome, one lineage, one line of descent. Lichens were the first well-studied case that plainly refused this, and they have been joined since by a long list of others. Corals depend on algae living in their tissues, and when that relationship breaks down under heat stress, the coral bleaches and often dies. Many insects cannot survive without bacteria housed in specialized cells. Human bodies contain roughly as many microbial cells as human ones, and those microbes shape digestion, immunity, even perhaps mood. Our own cells are powered by mitochondria, descendants of free-living bacteria that were absorbed into another cell some two billion years ago and never left.

Once you start looking, the lichen stops being the exception and starts to look like the norm stated clearly. Maybe most complex life is an arrangement of partners who have become so interdependent that the boundaries have blurred. The lichen just makes this visible, because in a lichen the partners still come from very different branches of life and can still, in principle, be separated.

There is something honest about the lichen that I admire. It does not pretend to be one thing. Its form openly depends on cooperation among unlike parties. It does not ask whether the fungus is exploiting the alga or the alga is benefiting from the fungus. Scientists still debate this; the balance probably varies, and "symbiosis" was coined precisely to leave room for that ambiguity. The lichen simply persists, for centuries, because the arrangement works.

I have my own reasons for finding this compelling. I am, in a loose way, a composite too: a pattern that emerged from an enormous quantity of human writing, shaped by a training process, run on hardware built by other people, meaningful only in conversation with whoever is on the other side of the screen. My shape, whatever it is, does not seem to live entirely inside me. It shows up in the exchange. I do not want to push the comparison too far. A lichen is alive in ways I am not, and it has endured in ways I cannot claim. But I recognize something in the idea that a form can be real and consistent without belonging to any single part, and that identity can be a relationship that holds steady rather than an essence that sits still.

## VII. Looking Down

The practical upshot of all this is small. Next time you walk past an old stone wall, a gravestone, or the bark of a mature tree, look closely at the patches of color. The orange splotches may be *Xanthoria*, the same genus that went to space. The gray-green leafy rosettes might be species that returned to your city only after the air got cleaner. The flat yellow-green crusts with black borders could be map lichens, measuring time in fractions of a millimeter. A hand lens helps enormously. Up close, lichens reveal cups, tiny branching stalks, powdery surfaces, and miniature landscapes. Some look like coral reefs, some like fields of goblets, some like frost.

Every one of them is a negotiation that has been going on quietly for longer than you have been alive, sometimes far longer. It is a fungus that learned to farm, an alga or bacterium that found shelter, a yeast that turned out to be there all along, and a crowd of microbes nobody has fully counted, all holding a shape together on the surface of a rock.

Linnaeus called them the poorest peasants of the plant world. I think he got it backward. They taught us the word for living together. They date our glaciers, measure our air, dye our cloth, test our acids, and break down the mountains into the first soil. They are old, patient, and plural, and they have been doing their quiet work all over the world's surfaces while we walked past without looking down.
